295.title: Philosophy for women too
295.hook: Musonius Rufus argued women should study philosophy as men do (Musonius Rufus, Lecture 3)
295.howItsDone: People of many backgrounds read the Stoics today, and some point to Musonius Rufus's lectures as an early argument that philosophy belongs to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the citadel, the mind free from runaway passions. Your line was one quiet room inside you.

Rome, in the age of the emperors. A girl learns to spin wool, run a household, keep accounts, and marry well. Her brother, if the family has money, learns rhetoric and philosophy. That's how things are usually done. Then a Stoic teacher stands up in front of his students and questions it. Not in a whisper: as a lecture, with arguments, one after another. His name was Musonius Rufus, and one of his students is someone this path has quoted again and again. This week, the Stoics honestly, starting with him.
screen: `ROME, IN THE AGE OF EMPERORS.` → `SPINNING FOR HER, BOOKS FOR HIM.` → `A TEACHER QUESTIONS IT.`

segments.voice: Musonius Rufus was a Roman Stoic who taught in Greek, was banished by emperors who found him inconvenient, and taught a young man named Epictetus. His lectures survive because a student wrote them down and a later collector, Stobaeus, preserved them. The third lecture asks whether women should study philosophy, and his answer is yes. The arguments are simple and sharp. Women have received from the gods the same power of reason as men. The same senses: sight, hearing, touch. The same natural desire for goodness, and they're just as pleased by fine and just actions. So why should it be fitting for men to seek how to live well, and not for women? In the next lecture he goes further: daughters should be educated the same way as sons, because the virtues, courage, justice, self-control, wisdom, are the same for everyone. Now the honesty this week promises. Musonius still pictured most women running households, and he thought some tasks suit men and some suit women. He wasn't arguing for everything people argue for today. But he did say the one thing that mattered most to a Stoic, virtue, belongs equally to both. And women had a place in this family of schools long before him: Hipparchia, the Cynic philosopher, married Crates, dressed like him, argued in public and was remembered for it. So in a school that says the only true good is character, the door to philosophy was, at least in principle, open to everyone with a mind. Philosophy for everyone.

Let the idea sit in your mind, ready to hand over.

296.title: Slave and emperor
296.hook: Epictetus enslaved, Marcus on the throne: one school, very different lives
296.howItsDone: Readers of Stoicism often study Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius side by side, and reflect on playing well the role life has handed them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musonius Rufus, who argued that philosophy belongs to women too. Your line was philosophy for everyone.

Two men. One was born into slavery, in a town in what's now Turkey: owned, sent where he was told, and, tradition says, walking with a limp. The other was born generations later into a wealthy Roman family, marked out young for the throne, and became emperor of Rome. Two lives could hardly be further apart. And yet the emperor learned how to live from the slave's words.
screen: `ONE BORN INTO SLAVERY.` → `ONE PICKED FOR THE THRONE.` → `SLAVE AND EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: The first man is Epictetus. Even his name carries his story: in Greek it means acquired, the kind of word you'd use for property. His owner, Epaphroditus, served at the court of Nero, and at some point the young man heard the lectures of Musonius Rufus, yesterday's teacher. Later he was freed. He taught in Rome until the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers, then opened a school in Nicopolis in Greece. He didn't write his teachings down himself: a student named Arrian did, and that's the Discourses and the Handbook this path keeps quoting. The second man is Marcus Aurelius. At the start of his Meditations he thanks the people who formed him, among them his tutor Rusticus, for introducing him to the discourses of Epictetus and lending him his own copy. So the emperor learned freedom from the notes of a former slave. And they teach the same thing: what's up to us is our own judgment and choice, and nothing else. Epictetus pictures it in his Handbook. You're an actor in a play, and the author gives out the parts: maybe a poor man, maybe a ruler, maybe someone who's lame. Your job is to play the part well; choosing it isn't yours. From a man handed slavery, that's not a slogan. To a man handed an empire, it's a warning not to confuse the costume with the person. One school, two very different parts, the same work.

297.title: Where they fell short
297.hook: the Stoics lived with slavery and empire, and admiring them doesn't mean agreeing with everything
297.howItsDone: Many modern readers of the Stoics keep their practical teachings while openly acknowledging the Stoics' acceptance of slavery and their entanglement with wealth and imperial power.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius, a former slave and an emperor in one school. Your line was the same school.

Everybody has had a hero who turned out to be a person. A coach, a grandparent, a musician whose songs got you through a hard year, and then one day you learn something about them that doesn't fit. What do you do with that? Throw them out entirely? Pretend you didn't hear it? There's a third way. This path has quoted the Stoics for most of a year, so i owe it to them, and to you, to try it here.
screen: `A HERO WHO TURNED OUT TO BE A PERSON.` → `THROW OUT, OR PRETEND?` → `A THIRD WAY.`

segments.voice: Start with slavery. The Stoics said all humans share the same reason, that we're citizens of one world, that a slave's mind is as free as an emperor's. And they lived in a society built on slavery and never, as far as we know, called for ending it. Seneca wrote a famous letter telling his friend to treat enslaved people as human beings: eat with them, speak kindly, remember that fortune could swap your places. That's real, and more than many Romans said. But Seneca himself owned many people, and the letter asks for kinder masters, not for no masters. Then wealth and power. Seneca was enormously rich while writing about the simple life, and he served as adviser to Nero. When Nero had his own mother killed, the historian Tacitus reports that Seneca was believed to have written the letter explaining it to the Senate. Marcus Aurelius spent much of his reign at war, and Christians were put to death in parts of the empire while he ruled; historians still debate how much he knew or directed. So what do we do? The Stoics hand us the tool themselves. Epictetus said no one is a finished sage; everyone is making progress, or not. They never claimed to be perfect. Admiring them honestly means keeping the teaching that holds, the dichotomy of control, the circles, the citadel, and naming plainly where they didn't live up to their own best ideas. Which raises an uncomfortable question: what will people three hundred years from now say we couldn't see?

segments.voice: Wonder about our own time: what do almost all of us accept, the way Romans accepted slavery, that people later might find hard to believe? Let one candidate come up; it doesn't need to be a perfect answer. Hold it without defending yourself or beating yourself up, and only notice.

Your line: honest admiration. The teaching can hold even where the teachers fell short. See you tomorrow.

298.title: Not a stiff upper lip
298.hook: in English "stoic" means unfeeling, which isn't what the Stoics meant
298.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners today distinguish apatheia, freedom from runaway passions, from apathy, and allow grief and love their honest place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seneca and the Stoics' blind spots, slavery, wealth and empire. Your line was honest admiration.

Read any sports page and you'll find it. The coach remained stoic after the loss. The widow was stoic at the funeral. In everyday English, stoic means jaw set, no tears, feelings locked in a box. Stiff upper lip. It's easy to assume that's the whole philosophy. After more than two weeks on the porch, you already know that's off. Today: how far off, and a future emperor who cried.
screen: `THE COACH REMAINED STOIC.` → `JAW SET, NO TEARS.` → `NOT A STIFF UPPER LIP.`

segments.voice: The confusion has a source. The Stoics' ideal was apatheia, freedom from pathos, the runaway passions we met two weeks ago. English turned that word into apathy, not caring at all, and turned stoic into unfeeling. But the actual goal was freedom from feelings built on false judgments, with room for good ones: joy, wise wishing, caution. Epictetus says it directly in his Discourses: a person shouldn't be unfeeling like a statue, but should keep up his natural relationships, as a son, a brother, a father, a citizen. A statue feels nothing. A Stoic loves his family. Then grief. Seneca wrote to a friend who had lost someone, and his advice was roughly: let the eyes not be dry, and don't let them flood either; you may weep, just don't wail without end. In the same letter he confesses that when his own dear friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept so much that he stands as an example of someone overcome by grief. A Stoic admitting it, in writing. And a late, not very reliable Roman history tells how young Marcus Aurelius wept at the death of his tutor, and courtiers tried to stop him. The emperor Antoninus said, roughly: let him be human; neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling. Whether or not it happened just that way, it's how that history remembers him. You may also meet a newer version online: Stoicism sold as never showing weakness, bottling everything up, or getting the upper hand on people. Plenty of readers of the old texts point out that it's close to the opposite: feel it first, then choose what to do. In these writers, the Stoic isn't the one with no tears. It's the one whose tears are honest, and who isn't swept away by them.

segments.voice: Find one feeling that's actually here right now, tiredness, sadness, hope, relief, anything, and name it quietly. Instead of managing it, let it be felt fully, the way you'd let a wave reach the shore: where is it in your body, and how big is it, really? Stay with it, breathing, not pushing it away and not feeding it.
Apatheia, the Stoics' ideal of freedom from runaway passions, not from feeling: honest tears, and a steady center.
Your line: not unfeeling. A Stoic can cry, and still stand steady. Day two hundred ninety-eight, done.

299.title: Plain food, hard ground
299.hook: Musonius taught plain food and hard work as training (Musonius Rufus, Lectures 18–19)
299.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners keep simple meals and occasional small hardships, like a cold shower or a plain lunch, as training in contentment rather than as punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: apatheia. The Stoics weren't unfeeling: honest tears, a steady center. Your line was not unfeeling.

Count the decisions food asks of you in a day. What to order. Which of the forty cereals. Whether the coffee has the right milk. Delivery or pickup. The next small pleasure is always one tap away, and the choosing never quite stops. In imperial Rome, a teacher looked at the rich tables of his city, dish after imported dish, feasts that ran for hours, and gave his students some unfashionable advice.
screen: `FORTY KINDS OF CEREAL.` → `ONE TAP AWAY.` → `PLAIN FOOD.`

segments.voice: That teacher was Musonius Rufus, whom we met four days ago arguing that women should study philosophy. Two of his lectures are about food, and he says something that sounds too simple: self-control at the table is the beginning and the foundation of self-control everywhere else. Why food? Because it comes around several times a day, a test you meet over and over. His advice is concrete. Prefer food that's cheap and easy to find: fruit, vegetables, milk, cheese, honey. Eat to nourish the body, not to chase the next flavor. He repeats an old saying often credited to Socrates: most people live to eat, but a good person eats to live. In another lecture he turns to clothing and houses. Clothes are for protecting the body, not for showing off; a house is for shelter from heat and cold, not for being admired. And in a lecture on training, he says a person should get used to cold and heat, thirst and hunger, a hard bed and plain meals, not as punishment, but as practice. The Greek word is askēsis, training, the word athletes used; it's where English gets ascetic. For Musonius, plain food isn't about being miserable, or saving money, or looking virtuous. It's a gym. Each simple meal is a small rep that makes you less easy to push around by wanting. His point: someone content with bread and cheese is harder to bribe, easier to please, and freer. Plain is training.

segments.voice: If you have water nearby, take one slow sip; if not, just swallow, and notice: nothing fancy, and yet exactly what the body wants. Now picture a plain meal, bread, rice, an apple, whatever is simple where you live, eaten slowly with no screen and no sauce. Notice any part of you that protests: that's the muscle.
Plain food. Musonius Rufus's training: simple meals and a little hardship, practiced so wanting has less hold on you.

300.title: Is this what I feared?
300.hook: Seneca: set aside days to live on very little and ask if this is what you dreaded (Letters 18)
300.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners set aside occasional days of voluntary discomfort, like simple food or skipping a convenience, to see that what they fear losing is survivable.

segments.voice: Yesterday: plain food, Musonius's training at the table. Your line was plain is training.

Day three hundred. Worth a breath of its own. Now a quieter question, one that can sit in the back of a mind for years: what if it all went away? The job, the savings, the comfortable apartment. What if I ended up with almost nothing? A fear like that can go unexamined, humming, shaping choices. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius in the middle of a noisy Roman holiday, suggested an experiment. Not thinking about the fear. Trying it, on purpose, for a few days.
screen: `DAY THREE HUNDRED.` → `WHAT IF IT ALL WENT AWAY?` → `TRY IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: It's December in Rome, the festival of Saturnalia. The whole city is feasting; Seneca writes that Rome is sweating with it. In the middle of this he writes his eighteenth letter. His advice: set aside a certain number of days, and live on the scantiest, cheapest food, in rough, coarse clothing. And while you do, ask one question. In Richard Gummere's translation of 1917: "Is this the condition that I feared?" His reason is a picture everyone in Rome would know. Soldiers practice maneuvers in peacetime, digging trenches with no enemy in sight, so they won't panic when the real day comes. The soul should do the same in good times: train while fortune is kind, for the day fortune isn't. And it shouldn't be a show, like rich Romans who played at poverty in fancy little rooms. Make the bed really hard and the bread really coarse. A lovely detail: in the same letter Seneca quotes Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, who kept certain days of eating very little to see whether he was missing any real pleasure. Seneca borrows good ideas wherever he finds them, and says so. His bet is that the trial teaches something. The thing dreaded turns out to be survivable, even ordinary. Plain bread is still bread. A cold room is still a room. And a fear looked at in daylight has less room to hum. The point isn't to lose everything. It's to find out, ahead of time, what you'd still have.
screen: `SATURNALIA: ROME IS FEASTING.` · `LIVE ON VERY LITTLE FOR A FEW DAYS.` · `SOLDIERS DRILL IN PEACETIME.` · `SENECA QUOTES EPICURUS.` · then, large: `IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?`

segments.voice: Picture one small but real comfort, the second coffee, the phone at lunch, the car for a short trip, the soft chair, and imagine the moment you go without it. Let the little pang come. Then ask Seneca's question gently, and stay with whatever answer comes: is this what I feared?
Saturnalia, the Roman December feast when Seneca urged practicing poverty on purpose, so fear loses its grip in good times.
Your line: plain bread is still bread. Three hundred days, and i'm glad for every one of them.

301.title: The Stoic day
301.hook: morning preview, attention through the day, evening review
301.howItsDone: Some modern Stoics keep a short morning reflection, check in with themselves during the day, and write or think through an evening review before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Saturnalia, and Seneca's question, is this what I feared? Your line was plain bread is still bread.

Three weeks on the porch. What the Stoics called good, how they saw feelings, their picture of the world, and this week, the Stoics honestly: Musonius arguing for women's education, a slave and an emperor in one school, where they fell short, their real tears, plain food, and Seneca's question. Big ideas, all of them. But a philosophy that lives only in your head is a hobby. The Stoics wanted it in your calendar, from waking to sleep. So before we turn to the science, here it all is in one ordinary day.
screen: `THREE WEEKS ON THE PORCH.` → `A PHILOSOPHY IN YOUR HEAD IS A HOBBY.` → `ONE ORDINARY DAY.`

segments.voice: The Stoic day has three parts, and you've met each one on this path. First, the morning preview. Marcus Aurelius starts book two of his notebook this way, in George Long's translation: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." It sounds grim, but he goes on: they act this way because they don't know good from bad, and they're my kin, so I can't be harmed by them or angry with them. It's a weather forecast for people, so the storm doesn't surprise you. Second, attention through the day. Epictetus has a whole talk on it; the Greek word is prosochē, attention, paying heed. His warning is practical: let your attention slip for a moment, and don't imagine you'll pick it up again whenever you like. Carelessness today makes tomorrow's carelessness easier. So through the day, the Stoic keeps checking: is this up to me? What am I telling myself? Is this the jolt, or the yes? Third, the evening review. Seneca describes how his teacher Sextius, every night before sleep, questioned himself: what bad habit did I cure today? What fault did I resist? In what way am I better? Seneca does the same, when the lamp is out and his wife has fallen silent, and then he forgives himself and resolves to do better. Morning, you prepare. Daytime, you notice. Evening, you look back kindly and learn. None of it takes long, and together they make a whole day into practice.
screen: `MORNING: THE PREVIEW.` · `DAYTIME: PROSOCHĒ, ATTENTION.` · `EVENING: THE REVIEW.` · `PREPARE, NOTICE, LOOK BACK KINDLY.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE DAY.`

segments.voice: Preview: picture the next few hours, and meet whoever might test your patience kindly, in advance. Attention: come right here, to this breath, and this one. Review: one thing from today that went well and one to do better; forgive it, and rest.
Prosochē, Epictetus' word for attention through the day, alongside a morning preview and evening review: the whole philosophy in one ordinary day.
Your line: the whole day. That closes three weeks on the porch; next comes the science of practice. Day three hundred one, complete.
